43. For the days shall come upon thee. He now assumes, as it were, the character of a judge, and addresses Jerusalem with greater severity. In like manner the prophets also, though they shed tears over the destruction of those about whom they ought to feel anxiety, yet they summon up courage to pronounce severe threatenings, because they know that not only are they commanded to watch over the salvation of men, but that they have also been appointed to be the heralds of the judgment of God. Under these terms Jesus declares that Jerusalem will suffer dreadful punishment, because she did not know the time of her visitation; that is, because she despised the Redeemer who had been exhibited to her, and did not embrace his grace. Let the fearful nature of the punishments which she endured now alarm us, that we may not, by our carelessness, extinguish the light of salvation, but may be careful to receive the grace of God, and may even run with rigor to meet it.

Luke 19:47. And he taught daily in the temple. Mark and Luke point out, first, what was the class of men of which the Church consisted, namely, of the despised multitude; and again, what enemies Christ had, namely, the priests and scribes, and all the rulers. Now this is a part of the folly of the cross, that God, passing by the excellence of the world, chooses what is foolish, weak, and despised. Secondly, they relate that those worthy guardians of the Church of God sought an occasion of putting Christ to death, by which their wicked impiety was discovered; for though there had been good grounds for pursuing Christ, yet they had no right to proceed to murder after the manner of robbers, or secretly to hire assassins. Thirdly, they show that the wicked conspiracy of those men was frustrated, because, by the secret purpose of God, Christ was appointed to the death of the cross.

               <ns0:p n="2">2 And behold, <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> a man named Zaccheus, which was the chief among the publicanes, and he was rich.<ns0:note place="bottom">We have had frequent occasions to hint, that the <ns0:hi>Publicanes</ns0:hi> were the gatherers of the <ns0:hi>Publick Revenue</ns0:hi> from the <ns0:hi>Romans.</ns0:hi> A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst them there was an order of Superiour and Inferiour Of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ficers: <ns0:hi>Zaccheus</ns0:hi> was the chief of them that were in that Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mission. <ns0:hi>And he was Rich,</ns0:hi> which is not to be wondered at, considering his employment, and is particularly mentioned doubt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />less to Magnify the Grace of God towards him, (of which we shall by and by hear more.)                <ns0:p n="4">4 And he ran before, and climbed up into a syco<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />more-tree to see him; for he was to pass that way.<ns0:note place="bottom">All this was but Curiosity, he saw a great Croud passing by, and asks what was the matter.                <ns0:p n="5">5 And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zaccheus, make hast, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house.<ns0:note place="bottom">I see no ground for their Opinion who think that before this time, <ns0:hi>Zaccheus</ns0:hi> his heart was touched with any love, or affection to Christ. The Evangelist seemeth to represent <ns0:hi>Zaccheus</ns0:hi> before this, as a meer stranger to Christ, <ns0:hi>he sought to see who he was.</ns0:hi> But Christ's <ns0:hi>looks</ns0:hi> are healing looks, there went vertue along with them to convert <ns0:hi>Zaccheus</ns0:hi> tho a Publican, and to recover <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> who had denied his <ns0:hi>Master,</ns0:hi> but they must be such <ns0:hi>looks,</ns0:hi> as carried with them a design to do good to Souls. Christ looked upon thou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sands to whom his looks conveyed no spiritual saving Grace. He that could heal by the hemm of his Garment touched, could change an heart by his look. How good a thing it is to be near the place where Christ is, what ever principle brings Men thither? provided Men come not as the Pharisees used to come, to execute their Malice. <ns0:hi>Zaccheus</ns0:hi> was brought to the bodily view of Christ, out of meer <ns0:hi>curiousity,</ns0:hi> but being there he receiveth a saving look from him, how many have had their hearts changed by <ns0:hi>Gospel</ns0:hi> Sermons, who never went to hear the Preachers with any such desire or design? O the freeness, and riches of Divine Grace! which seeketh not a wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thy object, but makes the object worthy, and therefore loveth it. <ns0:hi>What a Word was this. Come down for I must this Day abide at thine house?</ns0:hi>

               <ns0:p n="9">9 And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13.16.</ns0:note> the son of Abraham.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="11">11 And as they heard these things, he added, and spake a parable, because he was nigh to Jerusa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lem, and because they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear.<ns0:note place="bottom">We noted before, that <ns0:hi>Iericho</ns0:hi> was but 150 furlongs from <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rusalem,</ns0:hi> (which were not <ns0:hi>twenty Miles</ns0:hi>) and probably this dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />course was upon the way when he was come nearer to it. But the principal occasion of the following Parable was, his discerning of the Opinion which possessed some of the company which went along with him, that the time was now at hand when the <ns0:hi>Kingdom of God should appear.</ns0:hi> When Christ would put forth some emi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nent act of his Power, in delivering them from the servitude they were in, to the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> or in <ns0:hi>destroying</ns0:hi> the unbelieving Jews and Pharisees. Or when his Gospel should take a further place, and prevail in the World beyond what it yet had done. He there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore putteth forth a Parable to them, wherein by a familiar simi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />litude, he lets them understand, that he was going away from them, but would come again, and then receive the Kingdom. That in the mean time he would imploy them as his Servants, with his goods, and when he came would take an account what use, and improvement they had made of them, and then he would both reward his Friends, and be revenged on his Enemies.                <ns0:p n="27">27 But those mine enemies which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> before me.<ns0:note place="bottom">The Parable of the Talents which we had, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 25.14. is of great cognation to this Parable, and the Doctrine of it in many things is the very same; but the circumstances of that and this Relation, are so differing as I cannot think, that both <ns0:hi>Matthew</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> relate to the same time. I know nothing that hinders, but that our Saviour might twice repeat a Parable, which in sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stance is the same. Not to insist upon the examination of the Words used in the <ns0:hi>Greek,</ns0:hi> (which is a work fit only for <ns0:hi>Critical</ns0:hi> Writers) for the right understanding of this Parable we have three things to do. 1. To enquire what special instruction our Saviour did in this Parable intend to those who heard him at that time. 2. Who the Persons are represented in it, under the Notion of a Nobleman, and Servants, and what the things are, represented under the Notion, <ns0:hi>of going into afar Country, to receive a King<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom,</ns0:hi> distributing his Goods, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 3. What general instructions from it may be Collected, which are informative of us as well as those to whom our Lord at that time spake. The special in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />structions which our Lord in this Parable seemeth by it to have given his Disciples were these. 1. That they were mistaken in their Notions, or apprehensions of the sudden coming of Christs Kingdom in Power and Glory. He had first a great journey to go, and they had a great deal of work to do. Instead of Reigning amongst them, and exalting them, he was going away from them for a long time. 2. That there would be such a manifestation of his Kingdom in Glory and Power, when he should exalt and libe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rally reward his Friends, and severely punish all such as should be his Enemies. In order to these instructions, he taketh up this <ns0:hi>Parable,</ns0:hi> or speaketh to them in the use of this similitude. 3. As to the aptness of it. 1. The Nobleman here mentioned was Christ, who shall hereafter be a King in the exercise of Power and Justice, and distribute eternal Rewards and Punishments, but in his state of humiliation in which he was, when he thus spake to them was but <ns0:hi>like a Nobleman,</ns0:hi> a Son of Man, tho the chiefest of ten thousand. His <ns0:hi>going into a far Country,</ns0:hi> signifieth his going from Earth to Heaven. <ns0:hi>To receive a Kingdom,</ns0:hi> a Kingdom of Glory, Ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nour, and Power at the right hand of the Father. <ns0:hi>His returning</ns0:hi> signifies his coming again to <ns0:hi>Iudge the World at the last Day. His calling his Servants, and delivering to them ten Pounds,</ns0:hi> signifieth his giving <ns0:hi>Gifts unto Men,</ns0:hi> when he should <ns0:hi>ascend up on High,</ns0:hi> Gifts of several Natures, but all to be <ns0:hi>Occupied,</ns0:hi> used in a spiritual Trade, for the advantage of our common Lord. Not that he giveth to all alike (which it is manifest he doth not) for every passage in a Parable is not answered in the thing, which it is brought to represent or express. <ns0:hi>The Citizens hating him, and sending a Message after him,</ns0:hi> &c. signifies that the generality of the World are haters of Christ, and demonstrate their hatred by their refusal of his spiritual Government and Jurisdiction. <ns0:hi>His returning, and calling his Servants to an account,</ns0:hi> signifies, that when Christ at the last Day shall come to Judge the World, he will have an account of every individual Person, how they have used the Gifts with which he hath intrusted them, whither they be longer time of Life, more health than others, Riches, Honours, or more spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual Gifts, such as Knowledge, Utterance, Wit, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> or any trusty places, or Offices, they have been in. The <ns0:hi>different ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count</ns0:hi> the Servants brought in, signifieth, that Men do not equally use the Gifts with which the Lord blesseth them; some use them well, some ill, some bring Honour and Glory to God by the use of them, and that some in one degree, and some in another. Some bring him no Honour or Glory at all. The Masters answer to them upon their accounts, let us know that <ns0:hi>every Man shall be rewarded according to his Work.</ns0:hi> There will be degrees in Glory, (tho we cannot well open them) as well as of Punishments. <ns0:hi>The unprofitable Servants excuse for himself,</ns0:hi> signifies, the great itch of Proud Humane Nature to excuse it self, and lay all the blame of its miscarriages on God, either his severity, or his not giving them enough, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Kings answer, v.</ns0:hi> 22, 23. lets us know, that Sinners will be found to be Condemned out of their own Mouths. At the last Day, God will be found a Righteous God, and Man will be found to be the Liar. What the Lord further adds, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 24, 25. Lets us know Gods liberality in rewarding his Saints at last. What he saith, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27. concerning his Enemies assures us. That altho God spareth Men and Women a long time, so long as while his Son is in the <ns0:hi>far Country,</ns0:hi> while the Heavens must contain him; yet in the Day of Judgment, a most certain final ruin will be their portion. Hence we may easily gather what instructions are offered us in this Parable. 1. That the state of Christ when he shall come to Judge the World, will be a far more Glorious State, then it was while he was here upon the Earth. He was here in the appearance of a Nobleman, but he shall then appear as a King. 2. That all the good things which we have in this Life, are our Lords goods but in trust with us to be used for his Honour and Glory. 3. That it must be expected that in the World, there should be a great many Rebels against Christ and his Kingdom, a great many that shall say, <ns0:hi>We will not have this Man to rule over us.</ns0:hi> 4. That some make greater improvements then others, of what God in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trusteth them with for his Honour and Glory, and some make no improvement at all of them. 5. That Christ when he cometh to Judge the World, will have a strist account how Men have used his Goods, their time of Life, or Health, their Capacities, Ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nours, Riches, Trusts, Parts, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> 6. That those shall have the highest reward in Glory, who have made the highest improvements; but those who have made improvements in any proportion shall have their reward. 7. That Proud and Wretched Sinners, will think in the Day of Judgment to wipe their own Mouths, and lay all the blame of their miscariages on God. 8. That this is their folly, God will Condemn them from their own vain Pleas. 9. That in the Day of Judgment unprofitable Creatures, will, besides the loss of those Rewards which they might have received from God, have all their little satisfactions taken from them, in the enjoy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments of which they dishonoured God. 10. That tho Proud Sinners here oppose the Law of God revealed to them, and will not suffer Christ to Reign over them; yet his Power they shall not be able to resist, they shall at the last Day be slain before Christs face, and become <ns0:hi>his Footstool. He shall break them with a rod of Iron, and dash them in pieces like a Potters Vessel,</ns0:hi> Psal. 2.9. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 110.1. <ns0:hi>and who shall then deliver them out of his hand</ns0:hi>?</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="39">39 And some of the Pharisees from among the multitude said unto him, Master, rebuke thy disci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ples.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="40">40 And he answered, and said unto them, I tell you, that if these should hold their peace, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Heb. 2.1</ns0:note> the stones would immediately cry out.<ns0:note place="bottom">How Peevish were these wretched Pharisees? to envy our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour this little Triumph; of coming into the City upon an <ns0:hi>Asses colt,</ns0:hi> with Garments under him instead of a <ns0:hi>Saddle,</ns0:hi> or any stately furniture, and trappings, and attended by a Company of poor People throwing their Garments, and boughs of trees in the way; yet these they would have silenced. Our Saviours reply, <ns0:hi>If these should hold their Peace, the stones would immediately cry out.</ns0:hi> It seemeth to have been a Proverbial Speech used amongst them, to signifie a thing which could not be. This Day was accomplished Gods decree in that particular passage of Providence, concerning our Saviour, which could not be defeated.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="41">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:321" />41 And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it,<ns0:note place="bottom">Those who of old blotted out this Sentence, as thinking that weeping was not becoming Christs Perfection, seem to have for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gotten that he was <ns0:hi>perfect Man,</ns0:hi> and a sharer in all the natural in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">

                     </ns0:gap>rmities of humane Nature, (if <ns0:hi>weeping</ns0:hi> upon the prospect of Humane miseries, deserveth no better Name then an infirmity, being an indication of Love and Compassion.) Those who think that it was idle for him to <ns0:hi>Weep,</ns0:hi> for that which he might easily have helped, seem to oblige God to give out of his Grace, whether Men do what he hath commanded them and is in their Power to do yea or no Christ wept over <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> as a Man, compassionat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing these poor Jews, with respect to the Miseries he saw coming upon them. As a Minister of the Gospel pitying the People to whom he was primarily sent.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="42">42 Saying, if thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things <ns0:hi>which belong</ns0:hi> unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes.<ns0:note place="bottom">Speeches which are the products of great passion, are usually ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rupt and imperfect. <ns0:hi>If thou hadst known,</ns0:hi> That is, <ns0:hi>O that thou hadst known,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>I wish that thou hadst known.</ns0:hi> We are said in Scripture to know more than we believe, are affected with, and live up to the knowledge of. They had heard enough of the things which concerned their Peace; Christ had told them to them, but they attended not to them, they believed them not, and so cared not to direct their lives according to any such notions. <ns0:hi>At least in this thy Day.</ns0:hi> The time in which I have been Preaching the Gospel to thee, (for so I had rather interprete it, then of this last journey of our Saviours to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi>) This was properly the Jews day; for the first Preachers of the Gospel, spent all their time and pains amongst them. <ns0:hi>The things which belong to thy Peace,</ns0:hi> that is, to thy happiness, for so the term often signifies, and it referreth as well to the happiness of the outward, as of their inward Man, <ns0:hi>But now they are hid from thine Eyes.</ns0:hi> God will not suffer <ns0:hi>his Spirit always to strive with Man, because he is but Flesh,</ns0:hi> not fit to be always waited on by the great Majesty of Heaven. Fir<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t, Men shut their Eyes against the things that do concern their Peace, then God hideth them from them. No Man hath more then <ns0:hi>his Day,</ns0:hi> his time of Grace, how long that is none can tell, if he sleepeth out that, his case is desperate, past remedy.</ns0:note>

Chap. 21.6.</ns0:note> shall not leave in thee one stone upon another: because thou knew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est not the time of thy visitation.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is a plain Prophecy of the final Destruction of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> by the <ns0:hi>Roman Armies,</ns0:hi> which came to pass within less then forty years after. The cause of that dreadful judgment is assigned, <ns0:hi>because thou knewest not the time of thy Visitation.</ns0:hi> Gods visi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tations are either of Wrath or Mercy, <ns0:hi>of Wrath, Exod.</ns0:hi> 32.34. <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 26.16. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 15.3. <ns0:hi>of Mercy Ier.</ns0:hi> 29.10. It is plain that our Saviour useth the term here in the latter not the former sense, and that by Gods Visitation of this People here, is meant his visiting them with his <ns0:hi>Prophets,</ns0:hi> by <ns0:hi>Iohn the Baptist,</ns0:hi> and by himself. Their not knowing of it, (here intended) was their not making use of it, not receiving, and imbracing the Gospel. The contempt of the Gospel is the great cause of all those Miseries which come upon People in this Life, or shall come upon them in that Life which is to come.</ns0:note>
